newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Bank seeks to play down Horlick damage.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Bank seeks to play down Horlick damage.

text.p: Deutsche Bank sought on Friday to play down the second blow to its image in months, but analysts said the loss of a top London fund manager would not derail efforts to turn itself into a global investment bank.

British fund manager Nicola Horlick quit Deutsche's London-based investment banking arm, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, on Thursday after being suspended amid allegations she tried to persuade colleagues to join a rival company.
The highly-paid fund manager denied that allegation on Friday and travelled to Frankfurt to meet Deutsche's management board.
But the bank said the management board would refuse to meet Horlick and played down the impact of her departure as common in London's fast-moving investment banking scene.
"For anyone who is experienced in the investment banking business this kind of thing is an everyday occurrence, it has been overblown," Deutsche's chief spokesman Hellmut Hartmann said.

Horlick's departure follows hard on the heels of news that Deutsche must pay record compensation of 200 million pounds ($334.5 million) for irregularities at its British fund management arm Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM).
Analysts said the double blow to the international image of Europe's largest bank showed problems were inevitable as it pursued a ferocious expansion in a highly competitive market.

The bad press may lead to the loss of some of MGAM's pension fund business, they said. But the matter in no way suggested Deutsche's aggressive and costly expansion was proving more trouble than it was worth.
MGAM management chief Robert Smith told staff on Friday that Horlick had been suspended on Tuesday for "soliciting senior colleagues to join a competitor."
But Horlick said on arrival in Frankfurt she had been suspended on the basis of hearsay.

"There has been a very large misunderstanding, they should have asked me, they decided to suspend me on the basis of hearsay. That is appalling. I am sorry, I am not going to be treated like this," she told reporters.
Hartmann said the London and New York investment banking markets saw far higher staff turnover than Germany because of differences in mentality and fierce competition among banks and their staff.
The most important activities of Morgan Grenfell were now in place, he said, although it was still expanding its UK equities business.
"All the rest will now be organic growth," Hartmann said.

With returns from its costly domestic branch network likely to remain meagre, Deutsche must boost its income from the more lucrative business of issuing and trading in shares and bonds and managing funds, analysts said.
That means going to financial centres like London and New York, where the bulk of such business is done.

"With Morgan Grenfell, Deutsche will benefit from the move towards a stronger equity culture in Europe and I believe that by 1999 it will have pushed its way up to be among the top five investment banks in the world," said Stefan Ermisch, bank analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank.
"They have the power to do that but it's not a one-way street, there will be setbacks and these tend to be in the area of personnel."
Deutsche has been frequently accused itself of poaching staff from rivals with the lure of "telephone number" salaries and bonuses.
It has spared no expense hiring specialists and buying computerised trading equipment in an expansion launched in 1994 at Morgan Grenfell, which it bought in 1989.
It planned to spend 700 million marks ($436.4 million) in 1996 on hiring specialists and buying trading equipment. That outlay comes on top of costs in 1994 estimated at 1.7 billion marks.
